content: Personnel involved in toxicovigilance and public health should be adequately trained to identify and report cases that may indicate emerging hazards, outbreaks, or other events of public health significance. This training should follow a standardized operating procedure to ensure consistent and accurate reporting. Advanced training may be necessary to prepare for large-scale public health emergencies that require rapid coordination among multiple agencies, as outlined in specific guidelines. Staff must be well-versed in legislation and regulations concerning the safety of chemical products and pharmaceuticals. They should also be knowledgeable about local toxicological issues, such as those arising from environmental contamination or the misuse of psychoactive substances. Training should also include strategies for effective communication with the public, mass media, and professionals from other fields to disseminate prevention messages effectively. Poison centers require specific documentary resources and physical facilities to operate at a high standard. Additional resources beneficial for toxicovigilance and prevention activities include up-to-date contact lists, protocols, and procedures for information sharing, joint assessments, and coordinated event management. Reports from surveys and monitoring by other poison centers, as well as established programs for producing and distributing educational materials (e.g., brochures, videos, websites, mobile apps), are also essential. Poison centers should utilize educational materials from other centers and leverage social media and virtual forums to monitor and share information on medication misuse and substance abuse trends. Expertise in analyzing these media is crucial, and automated approaches like supervised classification and natural language processing show promise for future monitoring and interventions. Effective communication and coordination among all stakeholders in toxicovigilance and prevention are critical for planning and implementing these activities. National and international agreements significantly enhance the efficacy of toxicovigilance and poisoning prevention measures. Health ministries and public health agencies should advocate for, facilitate, endorse, and fund toxicovigilance and prevention activities. Improving the availability and accessibility of data on exposures and products is fundamental, and electronic records can streamline data storage, handling, and analysis. Official recognition of poison centers' roles in toxicovigilance and poisoning prevention adds authority to their preventive actions and facilitates access to comprehensive data on toxic and potentially toxic products. Poison centers' data and expertise can strengthen regulatory risk management measures. For instance, regulatory agencies considering changes to pharmaceutical restrictions should consult poison centers to assess the potential impact on poisoning incidence and monitor exposures post-implementation. At the national level, health ministries should enhance systems for collecting morbidity data on poisoned patients treated by healthcare professionals, ensure precise certification of mortality data by cause, and introduce mechanisms for mandatory notification of selected poisoning incidents. Regulations should require manufacturers to provide product information to a national database accessible to poison centers and health partners. Communication procedures between poison centers and national International Health Regulations (IHR) focal points should also be established. Poison centers should maintain industry contacts to exchange information on chemical and industrial products, their circumstances of use, and poisoning effects. They should promote the integration of data from related fields, contribute to a national toxicovigilance network supported by electronic communication tools, and facilitate information exchange and collaboration. At the international level, poison centers should have protocols to inform national IHR focal points about chemical threats with potential international implications, enabling information sharing with the World Health Organization (WHO) and other national focal points. Poison centers in different countries should share data on toxic risks to enable early warnings of potential problems. Standardized terminology, formats, and procedures for information exchange are essential for effective collaboration. International efforts should promote poison center networks, establish mechanisms for rapid notification of toxic alerts, and facilitate the exchange of education and training materials tailored for local use. In conclusion, poison centers play a vital role in global toxicovigilance by providing 24/7 services uniquely equipped to collect, analyze, and disseminate toxicovigilance data. Collaboration with other stakeholders enables near real-time detection of health threats and expert guidance for effective management and harm prevention.
